- fixes auth/profile loading so slow or failed profile fetches do not misroute users into onboarding
- hardens booking authorization, legal state transitions, cancellation windows, double-booking prevention, package-credit integrity, reviews, corporate RLS, and marketplace queries

fix(mcp): handle decoupled 3DS completion
## Intent
Make the operator COMPLETE decoupled / out-of-band (app-push) 3-D Secure, not just detect it.

Today the operator detects the 3DS challenge and waits, but for banks that authenticate the challenge OUT OF BAND (in a mobile banking app, decoupled 3DS) it never receives the completion, so the order never finalizes even though the bank authenticated successfully.
Live reproduction (3x, 2026-08-14): Merchant KobeeJapan (store.kobeejapan.net), single-page Shopify checkout, DBS Mastercard (vaulted), rc.21 installed (has #516 checkout fix + 3DS detection).

Operator fills card, submits, Stripe requires 3DS -> Stripe hosted challenge renders in a CardinalCommerce iframe (https://hooks.stripe.com/3d_secure_2/hosted?...payment_intent=pi_...&payment_intent_client_secret=...&publishable_key=pk_live_...&stripe_account=acct_...).
DBS uses decoupled/app-push 3DS: bank pushes to mobile app, user approves in-app out of band, bank/ACS authenticates OOB.
Bug: operator's in-browser challenge frame never receives that OOB completion -- operate_pay's three_ds_wait_seconds elapses and returns payment_3ds_required/needs_user (wall=3ds, resume=checkout).
Checkout stays stuck on Cardinal frame + Processing, no order is created, authenticated-but-uncaptured PaymentIntent expires uncaptured.
Verified the user approved the push immediately and it still never registered -- not a timing/latency problem, a missing completion path.

Root cause (confirmed via code read, not just hypothesis): the operator's 3DS handling (apps/mcp/src/bot/browser.ts detectThreeDsChallenge/waitForThreeDsResolution; apps/mcp/src/bot/pay-operator.ts 3DS state machine) only detected/finalized the IN-FRAME challenge-render case (user completes inside the iframe) via DOM text/URL heuristics, never the DECOUPLED case where completion is signalled server-side (Stripe transitions the PaymentIntent out of requires_action after the ACS confirms OOB).
It waited on an in-frame signal that never arrives for app-push banks.

Fix implemented: during the 3DS wait, additionally poll the authoritative Stripe PaymentIntent status -- the client_secret + publishable_key are already present in the challenge_url, parsed with a new parseStripeChallengeParams helper (publishable key only, never the secret key -- the same public retrieve-with-client-secret call Stripe.js itself makes client-side).

Chose PaymentIntent polling over polling Shopify's own checkout-completion internals because it's the same signal Stripe's SDK relies on, requires no per-merchant-theme reverse engineering, and needs no additional credentials.

When the PaymentIntent status leaves requires_action to succeeded/processing/requires_capture (classifyStripePaymentIntentStatus), that's treated as OOB-authenticated: the checkout page is reloaded once so the merchant's own completion logic re-evaluates now-authoritative server state, then the EXISTING DOM-based success detection (unchanged, still covers the in-frame case) gets a bounded ~30s grace window to confirm real order completion.
requires_payment_method/canceled PaymentIntent statuses are treated as a definitive failure.

Fail-closed: if the grace window elapses without a genuine DOM completion signal, the code returns a new distinct outcome (authenticated_pending_order -> payment_3ds_authenticated_pending_order) with needs_user guidance instead of ever silently claiming merchant/amount success on an unconfirmed completion.

Pivotick contains a DOM-based cross-site scripting vulnerability in its generic UI element resolution and icon-rendering utilities.
The tryResolveHTMLElement function treated any resolved string as HTML markup by assigning it to a <template> element through innerHTML.
Strings derived from untrusted graph properties or custom rendering callbacks could therefore introduce arbitrary HTML or SVG elements into the live document.
The vulnerable function was used by multiple UI components, including headers, property panels, extra panels, and tooltips.
Additionally, createIcon inserted caller-supplied svgIcon markup into a template without sanitization.
An application integrating Pivotick and deriving icon markup from untrusted data could therefore expose a second script-execution path.

An unauthenticated attacker able to provide a crafted graph, property value, rendering result, or SVG icon could execute JavaScript in another user's browser when the affected content is displayed or interacted with.
Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to access information available to the victim, manipulate graph data or application state, and perform actions with the victim's privileges.
The patch changes string rendering to use textContent, requiring callers to explicitly return an Element when HTML rendering is intended.
It also sanitizes SVG icon markup before inserting it into the DOM.

fix(realtime): prevent remote error payloads from crashing clients
## Summary

- Protect all five server-controlled Realtime error fields (`message`, `code`, `param`, `type`, and `event_id`) with exception-safe string conversion in the stable and beta handwritten Realtime emitters.
- Preserve existing valid-error formatting, the original event/error metadata, documented asynchronous rejection for unhandled errors, and exceptions thrown by application error listeners.
- Add one dedicated handwritten regression suite covering the four public stable/beta × native/Node WebSocket clients.
A remote WebSocket peer that can deliver a valid JSON Realtime error frame can send a noncoercible error value, for example:
The existing formatter interpolates attacker-controlled values before invoking registered SDK error handlers.

JavaScript coercion then throws `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value`; Node WebSocket clients can consequently terminate through an uncaught exception even when an SDK `.on('error')` listener is registered.
The same sink exists for all five error fields in both stable and beta clients.
The impact is remotely triggerable client denial of service, not credential disclosure or authentication bypass.
The fix catches only conversion failures and substitutes `[unserializable error value]`.

[CRITICAL] Enforced Authentication and Authorization for GraphQL Resolvers
📌 Description

This PR fixes a broken access control vulnerability in api/graphql_schema.py:208-302 and api/main.py:195-197 where GraphQL resolvers exposed application data and mutations without authentication or authorization enforcement.

Previously, the GraphQL implementation trusted attacker-controlled identifiers directly and exposed the schema publicly:

Resolvers accepted attacker-controlled user_id and case_id parameters
No authentication dependency was enforced
No ownership validation was performed
Arbitrary user data could be queried directly
Mutations operated on attacker-supplied resource identifiers
graphiql=True exposed the full schema publicly

Because the GraphQL API trusted user-supplied identifiers without validating authenticated user context or ownership, unauthenticated callers could query or modify arbitrary application data.

Current behavior before the fix:

Any user’s case data could be queried without authorization
Sensitive documents and records were exposed publicly
Mutations could modify or delete arbitrary application data
Authorization scope depended entirely on attacker-controlled input
GraphQL resolvers bypassed application access control guarantees
Public schema exposure simplified endpoint enumeration and exploitation

If an attacker submitted crafted GraphQL queries or mutations with arbitrary user_id or case_id values, they could retrieve or manipulate data belonging to other users without authentication.

As a result:

Any user’s case data could be queried without authorization
Sensitive documents and records could be exposed publicly
Unauthorized mutations could modify or delete arbitrary data
GraphQL became a direct broken-access-control vector
Complete application data compromise became possible
Authorization guarantees became inconsistent across API surfaces

The updated implementation enforces authenticated access, validates ownership consistently, and restricts GraphQL exposure to authorized application contexts.

With these changes:

GraphQL endpoints now require authenticated access
Resolvers enforce ownership and authorization checks consistently
User identity derives from authenticated session context
Attacker-supplied identifiers no longer determine authorization scope
Unauthorized queries and mutations are rejected safely
Production deployments restrict unnecessary schema exposure features

✨ Changes Included

Added authentication enforcement for GraphQL endpoints
Integrated ownership validation into GraphQL resolvers
Removed reliance on attacker-controlled authorization identifiers
Restricted unauthorized query and mutation access
Hardened GraphQL access control behavior across resolvers
Disabled unnecessary schema exposure features for production environments

🧪 Testing Done

Verified unauthenticated GraphQL requests are rejected correctly
Tested ownership enforcement across query and mutation resolvers
Confirmed unauthorized resource access is blocked safely
Validated authenticated users can access only permitted resources
Tested GraphQL mutation authorization behavior
Confirmed no regressions in authorized GraphQL functionality

closes #1215

atom 28: ldap-injection — LDAP injection
A corporate login (Flask + `ldap3`) authenticates against an OpenLDAP directory by concatenating untrusted input straight into an LDAP search filter — `(&(uid=<user>)(userPassword=<password>))` — and treating "the search matched" as a valid login.

Because an LDAP filter is structure (RFC 4515), a metacharacter in the input is read as syntax: sending `*` as the password turns the password check into the presence test `(userPassword=*)`, which matches `admin` and logs in without the password — an authentication bypass (A03 — Injection).

The fix escapes the RFC 4515 metacharacters (`escape_filter_chars`) on **both** `user` and `password` before the filter is built, so `*` becomes the literal `\2a` and the value is matched as data, never as filter structure.
The only difference in `app.py` is that one escape (plus the import).

Multi-container, following the datastore mold of `nosql-injection-mongo`: a shared OpenLDAP directory (built image, LDIF seed baked in, **no host port** — internal network only) plus `vulnerable` (127.0.0.1:8028) and `fixed` (127.0.0.1:8128).
`ldap3` is pure-Python, so no native `libldap`/toolchain is needed.

Same class, category, and ceiling (auth bypass) as `nosql-injection-mongo`, by a different engine and the *opposite* fix: there the injection was a type change and escaping was the wrong fix; here it is a metacharacter in a concatenated string and escaping is exactly the fix.

**Validation:** the app binds as a non-root service account (`cn=svc`) granted only `search` on `userPassword` via ACL — so the bypass is LDAP injection, not an over-privileged bind (an anonymous bind matches neither the honest baseline nor the payload).
Real filter logged on both sides: vulnerable `(&(uid=admin)(userPassword=*))` → `200`/`admin`; fixed `(&(uid=admin)(userPassword=\2a))` → `401`.
The honest string credential behaves identically on both sides; only the metacharacter payload separates them.
`ldap3` rejects the classic paren-injection with `LDAPInvalidFilterError`, so the working vector is the wildcard in a value position.

## The fix — escape the filter metacharacters
-    # VULNERABLE: user/password are concatenated straight into the LDAP search
-    # filter. ... the metacharacters * ( ) \ are syntax, not data ...
+    # FIXED: escape the RFC 4515 filter metacharacters in every untrusted value
+    # before building the filter. * ( ) \ become literal data (\2a \28 \29 \5c) ...

The vulnerable view concatenates `user` and `password` straight into the filter string. The fixed view runs each value through `escape_filter_chars` first, which replaces the RFC 4515 metacharacters `*`, `(`, `)`, `\` (and NUL) with their escape sequences `\2a`, `\28`, `\29`, `\5c` before they reach the filter. A `*` sent as the password is then no longer the wildcard that turns `(userPassword=<value>)` into a presence test — it becomes the literal search `(userPassword=\2a)`, matching only an account whose password is literally the one-character string `*` (there is none), so the login is refused. The value is matched as a value again. It escapes **both** `user` and `password`: both are attacker-controlled and both land in the filter, so both are escaped at the point of use.

An LDAP search filter is structure, and `ldap3` sends the filter string you hand it to the directory verbatim — it does not escape interpolated values for you. The vulnerable app builds the filter from raw input, so a metacharacter in the input becomes filter syntax. The fixed app guarantees every untrusted value is escaped before the filter is assembled, so the filter can only ever be the intended `(&(uid=<literal>)(userPassword=<literal>))` — two literal equality tests, with no room for a wildcard or a grafted-on clause. The benign case is unchanged: a real credential contains no metacharacters, so escaping is a no-op and it round-trips exactly as before. The root cause was never the character the attacker typed; it was concatenating untrusted input into the filter *as structure*, and escaping at the point of use is exactly its negation.
## Validating or blocklisting characters is not the fix

An experienced reader has a fix ready: "it's user input in a query — just restrict the characters, forbid `*` and parentheses in the `user` field." Whether you frame it as a blocklist of bad characters or an allowlist of good ones, it is the wrong shape. Policing the input's character set chases the form of the attack: alternate encodings, a metacharacter you forgot (`\`, NUL), a field that legitimately contains symbols, the next input you didn't think to filter. You stay one bypass behind, and you break real data that happens to contain a symbol.

Escaping is different in kind: it says "whatever this value contains, treat all of it as data," and it lives at the **point of use** — the moment the value is placed into the filter — so there is nothing to keep up to date and no legitimate input it rejects. Escape at the sink; don't try to sanitize the source. (Same shape as the "named, not applied" notes in `ssti-jinja` and `nosql-injection-mongo`: name the control the reader reaches for, and show why it is not the fix.)
## The honest design is a bind, not "the search matched"

One design note, because it is the tempting deeper fix and this atom deliberately leaves it alone. Deciding auth by *searching* `(&(uid=...)(userPassword=...))` and trusting that a match means a valid login is fragile on its own — it is what lets a filter trick become an auth bypass. Real LDAP authentication is a **bind**: the app connects to the directory *as the user's own DN* with the supplied password, and whether that bind succeeds *is* the password check. The injection in this atom — a metacharacter in the search filter — cannot produce a bypass against a bind, because the directory verifies the password itself instead of counting search hits.

So why keep the fragile design and only escape? Because switching to a bind changes the *design*, not the *vulnerability*. This atom isolates one flaw — untrusted input concatenated into a filter — and its minimal negation is to escape that input. Rewriting the login to bind would fix the injection only as a side effect of replacing the whole mechanism, which is exactly the kind of change that blurs what the lesson is. Name the better design; keep the diff to the cause. (Same spirit as the "hashing is orthogonal" note in `nosql-injection-mongo`.)
## Same class as the Mongo NoSQL injection — opposite fix

The finding is an authentication bypass: a crafted login as `admin` without the password, which is account takeover. That is the same ceiling as an auth bypass through SQL injection or NoSQL injection — and this atom is worth holding next to `nosql-injection-mongo` (22), because they are alike in impact and category and *nothing else*.
| Axis | SQL injection (`sqli-union-basic`) | NoSQL injection (`nosql-injection-mongo`) | LDAP injection (this atom) |
| Category | A03 — Injection | A03 — Injection | A03 — Injection |
| Query language | SQL — a string of commands | a MongoDB query — a JSON document | an LDAP search filter — a string (RFC 4515) |

| How input becomes structure | syntax spliced into a string (`' OR 1=1 --`) | type change: a string becomes an object carrying an operator (`{"$ne": null}`) | metacharacters in a concatenated filter string (`*` `(` `)` `\`) |
| The fix | parameterize (bind variables) | force the type (reject non-strings) | escape the RFC 4515 metacharacters |
| Is escaping the input the fix? | — | **no** — nothing to escape; the injection was a *type* | **yes** — the value carried filter *syntax* |

Read that last row across. In the Mongo atom, escaping is precisely *not* the fix: the injection was a value that changed type into an operator, there was no string to escape, and the fix was to force the type. Here the injection is a metacharacter inside a string the app concatenated, so escaping is *exactly* the fix. Same class — untrusted input becoming query structure in a query language that isn't SQL — but *how* the input becomes structure decides the remedy, and the remedy that missed in 22 is the one that lands here. "One atom, one vulnerability" is about the cause, not the impact: `sqli-union-basic`, `nosql-injection-mongo`, and this atom can all end in a subverted query and a bypassed login, by three different roots.

## O fix — escapar os metacaracteres do filtro
-    # VULNERABLE: user/password are concatenated straight into the LDAP search
-    # filter. ... the metacharacters * ( ) \ are syntax, not data ...
+    # FIXED: escape the RFC 4515 filter metacharacters in every untrusted value
+    # before building the filter. * ( ) \ become literal data (\2a \28 \29 \5c) ...

A view vulnerable concatena `user` e `password` direto na string do filtro. A view fixed passa cada valor antes pelo `escape_filter_chars`, que substitui os metacaracteres da RFC 4515 `*`, `(`, `)`, `\` (e NUL) pelas suas sequências de escape `\2a`, `\28`, `\29`, `\5c` antes de chegarem ao filtro. Um `*` mandado como senha deixa então de ser o curinga que transforma `(userPassword=<valor>)` num teste de presença — ele vira a busca literal `(userPassword=\2a)`, casando só uma conta cuja senha seja literalmente a string de um caractere `*` (não há nenhuma), então o login é recusado. O valor volta a ser casado como valor. O fix escapa **os dois**, `user` e `password`: ambos são controlados pelo atacante e ambos caem no filtro, então ambos são escapados no ponto de uso.
## Por que isso corrige o bug

Um filtro de busca LDAP é estrutura, e o `ldap3` manda a string de filtro que você entrega ao diretório verbatim — ele não escapa os valores interpolados por você. O app vulnerable monta o filtro a partir do input cru, então um metacaractere no input vira sintaxe do filtro. O app fixed garante que todo valor não-confiável é escapado antes de o filtro ser montado, então o filtro só pode ser o pretendido `(&(uid=<literal>)(userPassword=<literal>))` — duas igualdades literais, sem espaço para um curinga ou uma cláusula enxertada. O caso benigno fica inalterado: uma credencial real não tem metacaracteres, então escapar é um no-op e ela passa exatamente como antes. A causa raiz nunca foi o caractere que o atacante digitou; foi concatenar input não-confiável no filtro *como estrutura*, e escapar no ponto de uso é exatamente a negação disso.

Um leitor experiente tem um fix na ponta da língua: "é input de usuário numa query — é só restringir os caracteres, proibir `*` e parênteses no campo `user`." Seja como uma blocklist de caracteres ruins ou uma allowlist dos bons, é a forma errada. Policiar o charset do input persegue a forma do ataque: encodings alternativos, um metacaractere que você esqueceu (`\`, NUL), um campo que legitimamente contém símbolos, o próximo input que você não pensou em filtrar. Você fica um bypass atrás, e quebra dado real que por acaso contém um símbolo.

Escapar é diferente em natureza: ele diz "seja lá o que este valor contém, trate tudo como dado", e vive no **ponto de uso** — o momento em que o valor é colocado no filtro — então não há nada a manter atualizado e nenhum input legítimo que ele rejeite. Escape no sink; não tente sanitizar a source. (Mesma forma das notas "mencionável, não aplicada" do `ssti-jinja` e do `nosql-injection-mongo`: nomeie o controle que o leitor busca e mostre por que não é o fix.)
## O desenho honesto é um bind, não "a busca casou"

Uma nota de desenho, porque é o fix mais profundo e tentador e este átomo de propósito o deixa de lado. Decidir a auth *buscando* `(&(uid=...)(userPassword=...))` e confiar que um match significa um login válido é frágil por si só — é o que deixa um truque no filtro virar um bypass de auth. A autenticação LDAP de verdade é um **bind**: o app conecta ao diretório *como o próprio DN do usuário* com a senha fornecida, e o sucesso desse bind *é* a checagem de senha. A injeção deste átomo — um metacaractere no filtro de busca — não consegue produzir um bypass contra um bind, porque o diretório verifica a senha ele mesmo em vez de contar hits de busca.

Então por que manter o desenho frágil e só escapar? Porque trocar para um bind muda o *desenho*, não a *vulnerabilidade*. Este átomo isola uma falha — input não-confiável concatenado num filtro — e sua negação mínima é escapar esse input. Reescrever o login para bind corrigiria a injeção só como efeito colateral de substituir o mecanismo inteiro, que é exatamente o tipo de mudança que borra qual é a lição. Nomeie o desenho melhor; mantenha o diff na causa. (Mesmo espírito da nota "hashing é ortogonal" do `nosql-injection-mongo`.)
## Mesma classe do NoSQL injection do Mongo — fix oposto

O finding é um bypass de autenticação: um login forjado como `admin` sem a senha, o que é account takeover. É o mesmo teto de um bypass de auth via SQL injection ou NoSQL injection — e vale pôr este átomo ao lado do `nosql-injection-mongo` (22), porque eles são parecidos em impacto e categoria e *nada mais*.
| Eixo | SQL injection (`sqli-union-basic`) | NoSQL injection (`nosql-injection-mongo`) | LDAP injection (este átomo) |
| Categoria | A03 — Injection | A03 — Injection | A03 — Injection |
| Query-language | SQL — uma string de comandos | uma query MongoDB — um documento JSON | um filtro de busca LDAP — uma string (RFC 4515) |

| Como o input vira estrutura | sintaxe emendada numa string (`' OR 1=1 --`) | mudança de tipo: uma string vira um objeto carregando um operador (`{"$ne": null}`) | metacaracteres numa string de filtro concatenada (`*` `(` `)` `\`) |
| O fix | parametrizar (bind variables) | forçar o tipo (rejeitar não-string) | escapar os metacaracteres da RFC 4515 |
| Escapar o input é o fix? | — | **não** — não há o que escapar; a injeção era um *tipo* | **sim** — o valor carregava *sintaxe* de filtro |

Leia essa última linha de ponta a ponta. No átomo do Mongo, escapar é justamente *não* ser o fix: a injeção era um valor que mudava de tipo para um operador, não havia string para escapar, e o fix era forçar o tipo. Aqui a injeção é um metacaractere dentro de uma string que o app concatenou, então escapar é *exatamente* o fix. Mesma classe — input não-confiável virando estrutura de query numa query-language que não é SQL — mas *como* o input vira estrutura decide o remédio, e o remédio que errou no 22 é o que acerta aqui. "Um átomo = uma vuln" é sobre a causa, não sobre o impacto: `sqli-union-basic`, `nosql-injection-mongo` e este átomo podem todos terminar numa query subvertida e num login bypassado, por três causas diferentes.
> ⚠️ Intentionally vulnerable. Run locally only. Never expose to the internet or a shared network.

A minimal Flask + OpenLDAP lab for LDAP injection. A corporate-style login endpoint — `POST /login` — takes a `user` and a `password` and authenticates them against an LDAP directory: it builds a search filter and considers you logged in if the search returns anyone — `(&(uid=<user>)(userPassword=<password>))`. The catch is that an LDAP search filter is not inert text — it is **structure** (RFC 4515), and characters like `*`, `(`, `)` and `\` are *syntax*, not data. The endpoint pastes whatever the client sent straight into that filter, so those metacharacters are interpreted as filter logic. Send `*` as the password and the filter becomes `(&(uid=admin)(userPassword=*))` — "an `admin` that simply *has* a password" — and you log in as `admin` without knowing it.

The lesson is that the root cause is **concatenating untrusted input into the filter without escaping it**: the value stops being a value and becomes filter structure. The fix is not to validate or blocklist "weird" characters — it is to **escape the RFC 4515 metacharacters** (`escape_filter_chars`) in every untrusted value before the filter is built, so `*` `(` `)` `\` turn into literal data (`\2a` `\28` `\29` `\5c`) and the filter stays the one the code intended.

fix: support GeoLibre inside Power BI opaque sandbox
## Problem
GeoLibre works when opened directly and inside the HyperPBI Playground, but Power BI Desktop can leave the embedded component stuck at `Waiting for the pinned GeoLibre runtime handshake.`
Power BI can host custom visuals inside a sandboxed browsing context whose nested frames use an opaque serialized origin (`MessageEvent.origin === "null"`).
HyperPBI previously required every GeoLibre message to have the normal HTTPS origin, so it discarded the real `geolibre:ready` message even when it came from the exact GeoLibre iframe window.

- support two pinned message transports: normal HTTPS origin and opaque sandbox origin
- accept the opaque transport only from the exact GeoLibre iframe `contentWindow`
- pin the transport only after the expected GeoLibre version successfully completes the handshake
- prevent later messages from switching between strict and opaque origin modes
- use `postMessage(..., "*")` only after the opaque transport has been positively established; normal browser/runtime traffic remains exact-origin
- preserve project load/state and baseline selection events in the Power BI sandbox
- handle versioned `selectionChanged` events directly so GeoLibre -> Power BI interaction remains available without the public embed client
- add a managed-runtime fallback for `highlightFeature`, preserving Power BI/HyperPBI -> GeoLibre external highlighting when the public `@geolibre/embed` client cannot address an opaque child
- keep the public enhanced client for normal browser origins and keep it optional
- bump the PBIVIZ version to `1.0.1.3` so Power BI Desktop does not reuse the previous cached visual package
The change does **not** globally trust null origins.

HyperPBI still requires the message to come from the exact iframe WindowProxy, validates the pinned GeoLibre version before opening the opaque transport, then locks that transport for the lifetime of the adapter.
Unexpected HTTPS origins and origin-mode changes are rejected.

- normal HTTPS-origin behavior still rejects attacker/null-origin traffic
- Power BI-style opaque handshake loads the project and uses `*` only after validation
- project state and selection events round-trip over the opaque transport
- external feature highlights use the managed opaque embed-command fallback
- invalid null-origin versions cannot pin the transport
- existing enhanced API, slow-start, timeout, and terminal-runtime behavior remain covered

Harden app against common web attack vectors
## Summary
A full security-hardening pass across the backend API, frontend, and AI endpoints.
Six real, exploitable issues found and fixed:
- **Stored XSS (frontend)** — `escapeAttr()` only escaped `"`, giving effectively no protection in text-node `innerHTML` contexts (e.g.
Replaced with a proper `escapeHtml()` and applied it to every user-controlled render site, including several that had no escaping at all.
Verified with a live Playwright test confirming an injected `<script>` payload never executes.
- **Content-type confusion / stored XSS via file upload** — the server trusted and echoed back the client-declared multipart `Content-Type`.
Combined with the review UI's `blob:`-iframe document preview, this let an HTML/JS file disguised as a PDF execute same-origin when previewed.
Fixed by deriving content-type solely from a fixed extension→MIME allowlist server-side, never from client input.
- **Missing rate limiting** — login and signup had none (only forgot-password/reset/contact did); the AI assistant endpoint had none either, despite every call being billed Anthropic API spend.
Added a shared `createRateLimiter` factory, applied per-IP to login/signup and per-org to the assistant endpoint (the real cost there is API spend, not request volume).
- **No upload size limit** — unbounded uploads were a disk-exhaustion DoS vector.
Added a 20MB limit via multer with a clean `413` instead of a generic `500`.
- **CSV/Excel formula injection** — an exported cell starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` executes as a live formula in Excel/Sheets/LibreOffice, not as text.
A malicious vendor name or filename could exploit this the moment a finance team member opens their own export.
Fixed with the standard leading-apostrophe mitigation.

angular-server-side-configuration information disclosure vulnerability in monorepo with node.js backend
### Impact
angular-server-side-configuration detects used environment variables in TypeScript (.ts) files during build time of an Angular CLI project.
The detected environment variables are written to a ngssc.json file in the output directory.
During deployment of an Angular based app, the environment variables based on the variables from ngssc.json are inserted into the apps index.html (or defined index file).
With version 15 the environment variable detection was widened to the entire project, relative to the angular.json file from the Angular CLI.
In a monorepo setup, this could lead to environment variables intended for a backend/service to be detected and written to the ngssc.json, which would then be populated and exposed via index.html.
This has NO IMPACT, in a plain Angular project that has no backend component.

### Patches
Vulnerability has been mitigated in 15.1.0, by adding an option `searchPattern` which restricts the detection file range by default.

```bash
# Update via npm
npm update angular-server-side-configuration
## Or more specific
npm install angular-server-side-configuration@15.1.0

# Update via pnpm
pnpm update angular-server-side-configuration
## Or more specific
pnpm add angular-server-side-configuration@15.1.0

# Update via yarn
yarn update angular-server-side-configuration
## Or more specific
yarn add angular-server-side-configuration@15.1.0
```

### Workarounds
Manually edit or create ngssc.json or run a script after ngssc.json generation

source_security_narrative_excerpt:
Lack of SSL/TLS certificate and hostname validation in Amazon EC2 Plugin
Amazon EC2 Plugin connects to Windows agents via HTTPS.
Amazon EC2 Plugin 1.50.1 and earlier unconditionally accepts self-signed HTTPS certificates and does not perform hostname validation when connecting to Windows agents.
This lack of validation could be abused using a man-in-the-middle attack to intercept these connections to build agents.
Amazon EC2 Plugin 1.50.2 by default no longer accepts self-signed HTTPS certificates and performs hostname validation.
A new configuration option allows restoring the previous, unsafe behavior.
For more information see [the plugin documentation](https://github.com/jenkinsci/ec2-plugin/#securing-the-connection-to-windows-amis).
